title: Holy time, not holy place
hook: Shabbat is built in time; it begins at sundown on Friday and ends at nightfall Saturday

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mishkan, a dwelling built from everyone's gifts, and the end of camp two. Your line was build a place, presence comes. Today camp three begins: the practices. Day ninety-seven.

Think about where people go to feel close to something bigger. A cathedral. A mountaintop. A shrine at the end of a long road. Places you have to travel to. Now imagine a holy place you don't travel to at all, because it travels to you. It arrives every week, on the same day, wherever you are: a hospital room, a dorm, a kitchen in a small apartment. You can't buy a ticket to it and you can't be too far away from it. It just comes, at sundown, on Friday. Camp three is about the things Jews do, and it starts here. Today: holy time.
screen: `HOLY PLACES YOU TRAVEL TO.` → `A HOLY PLACE THAT COMES TO YOU.` → `EVERY FRIDAY, AT SUNDOWN.`

segments.voice: Go back to the first chapters of Genesis. God makes light, sky, sea, land, stars, animals and people, and calls them good. But the first thing the Torah calls holy isn't any of them. It's a day. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And God blessed the seventh day, and hallowed it." Hallowed means made holy, kadosh in Hebrew. Before there was a holy mountain or a holy tent, there was a holy time. The twentieth-century rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel built a whole book on that observation. He described Shabbat as a sanctuary built in time instead of in space, a palace people enter once a week and leave at the end of the day. We just spent a camp on the mishkan, a tent you could carry. Shabbat is even more portable. The Jewish day starts in the evening, because Genesis says there was evening and there was morning. So Shabbat begins at sundown on Friday. Many families light candles a little before sunset, and it ends on Saturday night when three stars can be seen in the sky. About twenty-five hours. In that time, observant Jews stop the kind of work that makes and changes the world, and spend the day on rest, meals, prayer, family, study and friends. Others keep parts of it: a Friday dinner, candles, an unplugged afternoon. Jewish movements differ on how Shabbat is kept, and many Jews find their own place on that range. What they share is the idea underneath it: some things can't be made in space. They can only be kept in time.
screen: `THE FIRST HOLY THING WAS A DAY.` · `A PALACE IN TIME.` · `SUNDOWN FRIDAY TO THREE STARS.` · `KEPT IN MANY WAYS.` · then, large: `AND GOD BLESSED THE SEVENTH DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one hour this week to make nothing. Settle, and breathe. Look at the week ahead the way you'd look at a calendar on the wall. Find one hour. It could be Friday night, or Saturday afternoon, or any hour that works for your life. In that hour you won't produce, fix, buy or post anything. Picture it: where you'd be, who'd be there, what you'd do instead. Then mark it, in your head or in your phone. The bell holds the time.
Holy time. Shabbat, the first thing the Torah calls holy: a day, not a place, from sundown Friday to nightfall Saturday.
Your line: holy time. Today, put your hour in the calendar and guard it the way you'd guard a trip to somewhere far away. Day ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Shabbat begins at sundown on Friday and ends when three stars appear on Saturday night; many Jewish families mark it with candles, a festive meal and a day set apart from work.

fork.setup: you're reading Genesis for the first time. God has made light, land, stars and people. what's the first thing called holy?
fork.reveal: "and God blessed the seventh day, and hallowed it": the first holy thing is a stretch of time.

original.note: Hebrew: holy, set apart. Kiddush and kedushah come from the same root.

trapdoor: what you thought: a day off.
what it means: a sanctuary in time, from sundown Friday to three stars on Saturday, set apart from making and changing the world.
what a scholar hears: Genesis 2:3 uses the root k-d-sh for the first time in the Torah for a day; Heschel's The Sabbath (1951) made 'a palace in time' famous.
